title: Taking a look at Cartaventura: Adventure Awaits: Vinland
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RrVaJ5z_3mU

Daniel (@dungeondive) takes a quick look at *Cartaventura: Adventure Awaits: Vinland* from Kosmos, a very small box that looks and plays like a simplified *7th Continent*. The rules fit on two cards, around seventy numbered cards form the "pages", and Daniel's verdict arrives early: this feels like a gamebook with the spine cut off and the pages laid on the table, and nothing is gained by playing it with cards instead of a book.

You play Leif Erikson, sailing from Iceland after failing to clear Erik the Red's name, home to a Greenland where Christianity is arriving and your mother has converted. Cards with a gear are actions; flipping to the black square marks a card's terminus. God cards (Loki, Thrud, Tyr) unlock gem-locked choices once you win their favour. Choosing one path discards the visible alternatives, so branches lock permanently, and the deck resets in number order for another run at one of five endings. Daniel notes the story handles real historical religious conflict frankly enough that it may unsettle some players.

The art is nice but purely decorative; unlike *7th Continent* there are no clues hidden in it, and no inventory or survival layer. At $14.95 it is a pleasant few hours, perhaps a good evening for two, but Daniel would point adventure-hungry buyers to *Fabled Lands: The Serpent King's Domain* for far more game at the same price.

----

If a card game gains nothing from being on the table, should it have been a book, or is the tabletop ritual itself worth something?
